definition: The nearly straight-line configuration of three celestial bodies — most often the Sun, Earth, and Moon — in the same gravitational system; by extension, any pairing or yoking of opposites into a unified whole.
etymology: From Greek suzugia, a joining together, built from sun- meaning with or together and zugon meaning yoke. That same zugon is the ancestor of the English word yoke itself, and of the zoo- root that gave us zygote — the original joined cell. The word traveled into Late Latin as syzygia before English astronomers adopted it in the seventeenth century to describe the Moon at its full and new phases, the two moments when Sun, Earth, and Moon pull into alignment.
usage: Syzygy arrives just as June slides toward its first full moon after the solstice, when the geometry of the solar system draws its players into something close to a line. It earns its place in the language twice over: as a precise term of orbital mechanics and as one of the few English words that strings three y's together without a single conventional vowel, a typographical curiosity that makes it a quiet favorite of word lovers and crossword constructors alike.
